findings.headline: Pension contribution rate increasing from 17.6% to 20% from April 2026 following triennial revaluation, removing buffering secondary contributions
findings.detail: The Local Government Pension Scheme triennial revaluation in 2025 resulted in a 2.4 percentage point increase in the primary employee contribution rate from 17.6% to 20%, effective 1 April 2026. The secondary cash contribution that previously buffered payroll fluctuations has been removed entirely. The council overspent on secondary contributions by £18,812 in 2025/26, showing the scheme was already under pressure.
findings.matters: This is a permanent, inflation-linked cost increase across the entire workforce with no offsetting reductions. The removal of secondary buffering exposes the council to future pension cost volatility.
findings.figures: Primary pension contribution rate 2015-2026: 17.6% (unchanged for six years). New rate from 1 April 2026: 20%. 2025/26 secondary contribution overspend: £18,812.
findings.quote: The pension scheme triennial revaluation was undertaken by the pension scheme actuaries and administrators in 2025 resulting in an increase in the primary contribution rate to 20% from the 1st April 2026 and the removal of the secondary contribution.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation crisis: 73 households costing £924,000 per year in lost Housing Benefit subsidy, with £3m capital programme to solve it only 44% spent
findings.detail: The council has 73 households in temporary accommodation (average 76 per year). Only 22 can be housed in council-owned emergency accommodation; the rest rely on Bed & Breakfast and hotels. The council can only recover 27% of the average weekly cost paid to private providers due to Housing Benefit subsidy rules. This cost the council £924,000 in lost subsidy in 2025/26. A capital programme to acquire 30 additional beds has spent only £1.335m of £3m approved, with slippage into 2026/27.
findings.matters: This is chronic revenue pressure that will persist until capital delivery completes (and even then, will only recover £361,000 of the £924,000 annual loss). The underspent capital programme shows housing acquisition targets are behind schedule, suggesting the crisis will worsen before it improves.
findings.figures: Current temporary accommodation: 73 households (annual average: 76). Lost Housing Benefit subsidy 2025/26: £924,000. Clawback rate on B&B/Hotel: 27%. Council-owned emergency capacity: 22 singles. Capital programme expenditure: £1.335m of £3m approved. Expected annual subsidy recovery when fully occupied: £361,000.
findings.quote: The reliance on Bed & Breakfast and Hotels to house an average of 54 clients cost the Council £924,000 in lost Housing Benefit Subsidy in 2025/26. For temporary accommodation not owned by the Council, we are only able to claw back around 27% of the average weekly cost we pay out.

findings.headline: Leisure contract income to drop by £1.39m annually from 2027/28 when the current contract ends, adding to the structural funding gap
findings.detail: The current leisure contract ends in 2026/27. The council is negotiating a new contract for 2027-2033 and is budgeting for a £1.39m annual income reduction. This permanent income loss is already factored into the MTFS funding gap. The council spent £83,000 in reserves during 2025/26 to fund legal and procurement costs for the new contract negotiation.
findings.matters: A £1.39m ongoing annual income loss from a service the council does not control (operated by a contractor) represents unrecoverable shrinkage in the revenue base and compounds the structural deficit.
findings.figures: Expected leisure income reduction from 2027/28 onwards: £1.39m per year. 2025/26 leisure contract income exceeded budget by £176,000 due to CPI adjustment. £83,000 of underspend reserved for new contract negotiation and procurement.
findings.quote: This excess income has been moved to earmarked reserves to help offset the £1.39m reduction in leisure income expected from 2027/28 following the negotiation of the new contract

findings.headline: Council cannot balance its budget from operations and will rely on reserve drawdown to fund a £3.28m structural revenue gap over three years
findings.detail: The Medium-Term Financial Strategy identifies a £3.28m funding gap over three years and £10.5m over five years, driven by the Business Rates reset, leisure contract income reduction, and government funding cuts. The council's stated strategy is to use General Fund and Earmarked Reserves to close this gap. This is not a temporary measure but the official plan for balancing budgets through 2029.
findings.matters: Reserve-funded deficits are finite and unsustainable. Continued reliance signals the council cannot operate within its means and eventually faces insolvency when reserves are exhausted.
findings.figures: MTFS revenue funding gap: £3.28m over 3 years, £10.5m over 5 years. 2025/26 contribution to General Fund: £203,155. Earmarked reserves at year-end before analysis: 45 separate reserves totalling £3,715,000 in new 2025/26 additions alone.
findings.quote: The Council will therefore need to rely on the General Fund and Earmarked Reserve balances to set a balanced budget over the life of the existing MTFS.

findings.headline: Retained Business Rates income will fall 66% in 2026/27 when the Government's Business Rates reset takes effect
findings.detail: Retained Business Rates income drops from £6.987m in 2025/26 to £2.4m in 2026/27. This is because the council was part of a Business Rates pool that generated gains via a reduced levy (£1.257m saving in 2025/26), but the reset removes this benefit entirely. This is a permanent structural funding loss, not a temporary fluctuation.
findings.matters: A two-thirds loss of a major funding stream forces the council into planned reserve drawdown to balance budgets, which is unsustainable and signals structural insolvency risk.
findings.figures: Retained Business Rates 2025/26: £6.987m; 2026/27 projection: £2.4m. 2025/26 Business Rates pool levy reduction: £1.257m (actual) vs £2.774m (budgeted). Deficit payable 2025/26: £687,000.
findings.quote: our retained Business Rates will drop to £2.4m in 2026/27 from £6.987m in 2025/26 (after movements to reserves to repay the 25/26 deficit).

findings.matters: Prudential indicators exist to bound risk. A breach signals either forecasting weakness (budget assumed lower balances than materialized) or that the council exceeded its own risk tolerance. The forecast assumes the council will manage this transition by borrowing externally rather than further depleting reserves.

findings.paper_title: Finance paper on Budget Amendments Proposed by the Conservative Group - 230226
findings.headline: General fund reserves would decline to £794,823 by 2030/31 if amendments accepted, down from £2,045,711 in the proposed budget.
findings.detail: Multiple amendments collectively reduce earmarked reserves and revenue resources. The combined impact shrinks the general fund balance by more than 60% over the MTFS period. This trajectory leaves minimal buffer for adverse events or spending pressures in later years.
findings.matters: Reserve adequacy is a key indicator of financial resilience for lenders and affects debt serviceability and the council's ability to absorb shocks.
findings.figures: General fund balance reduced to £794,823 by 2030/31 (from £2,045,711); amendments impact: earmarked reserves -£411,726, council tax income -£353,803 annually

findings.paper_title: Budget Paper for February Council - with final settlement figures
findings.headline: Contract inflation pressures: Ubico negotiations protracted, audit fees rising year-on-year due to complexity
findings.detail: Section 2.1 notes the Ubico contract "was initially included in the first draft of the budget as an increase of £319,784. Following extensive discussions this has reduced by £134,404 to £185,380." The negotiation was difficult and the increase remains material; the council cites fuel, vehicle repairs, and staffing. Separately, external audit fees are "set by the Public Sector Audit Appointments (PSAA)" but the council notes "the additional complexity of the audit work is reflected in the increasing cost year on year." These are externally-driven cost pressures.
findings.matters: Contracted services that the council does not fully control are experiencing cost drift; this limits the council's ability to manage budget surprises.
findings.figures: Ubico contract growth reduced from £319,784 to £185,380 for 2026/27; audit fees rising year-on-year
findings.quote: The Ubico contract was initially included in the first draft of the budget as an increase of £319,784. Following extensive discussions this has reduced by £134,404 to £185,380 for 2026/27. The key changes relate to fuel, vehicle repairs and staffing.

findings.paper_title: Budget Paper for February Council - with final settlement figures
findings.headline: Investment property income declining: two tenants leaving, £66,363 loss in 2026/27 plus ongoing impact
findings.detail: Section 2.1 notes: "It is expected that two tenants will be leaving at the end of their current lease. The figure of £66,363 represents the loss of rent and the liability for Business Rates that will be charged to the Council in the second half of the year." Earlier, section 4.3 notes the sale of Between Towns Road (Oxford office vacant since Nov 2023) for a one-off saving of £157,826. Investment property income is volatile and a shrinking contributor to the budget; section 4.3 shows budgeted income at £3,037,235 for 2026/27, so the loss is material (~2%).
findings.matters: Loss of rental income combines with reduced pool bonuses and falling investment returns; the council's commercial income base is contracting.
findings.figures: £66,363 loss in 2026/27 from two tenant departures; £3,037,235 total investment property income budget
findings.quote: It is expected that two tenants will be leaving at the end of their current lease. The figure of £66,363 represents the loss of rent and the liability for Business Rates that will be charged to the Council in the second half of the year.

findings.paper_title: Budget Paper for February Council - with final settlement figures
findings.headline: External borrowing deferred to 2027/28 due to better settlement, but capital programme scale will require PWLB borrowing at still-elevated rates
findings.detail: Section 9.2 states external borrowing was "initially thought" necessary in 2026/27 for waste vehicle fleet replacement, leisure centre improvements, and affordable housing, but a better-than-expected settlement allows deferral to 2027/28. However, section 9.4 notes "PWLB interest rates are still high but should fall gradually over the next 12 months." The capital programme cannot be deferred indefinitely; when borrowing is taken, rates are assumed to be higher than the council would prefer, and the revenue impact (interest + MRP) will hit an already-pressured MTFS.
findings.matters: The council has postponed but not avoided substantial borrowing; the timing creates a cliff risk if rates do not fall or if LGR delays push borrowing further out.
findings.figures: Borrowing deferred from 2026/27 to 2027/28; PWLB rates described as "still high"
findings.quote: The PWLB interest rates are still high but should fall gradually over the next 12 months in line with the expected trajectory of the Bank of England Base Rate.

findings.paper_title: Budget Paper for February Council - with final settlement figures
findings.headline: Reserves strategy flagged as unsustainable: council explicitly warns reserves cannot fund ongoing shortfalls
findings.detail: Section 3.11 states: "The use of reserves to manage short term fluctuations in the Council's financial position is necessary but cannot be sustained over the longer term – reserves can only be spent once." Yet the council's MTFS explicitly relies on earmarked reserves to bridge years 2-3 (due to £2.3m funding cut), and has now committed £1.5bn+ from 2026/27 revenue to specific projects (WESP and LGR phases) with funds "expected to be expended during the period 2026-2028."
findings.matters: The council is managing a structural funding shortfall using a one-time resource pool; this strategy has explicit end-date and no escape route if LGR costs exceed estimates.
findings.figures: £1,509,529 earmarked from 2026/27 budget for WESP and LGR phases
findings.quote: The use of reserves to manage short term fluctuations in the Council's financial position is necessary but cannot be sustained over the longer term – reserves can only be spent once.

findings.paper_title: Budget Paper for February Council - with final settlement figures
findings.headline: Business Rates Pool closing at end of 2025/26, removing multi-year income stream (£1.05m in 2024/25)
findings.detail: The Business Rates reset under the Fairer Funding Review removes the growth over baseline that has made pool membership profitable for the council. Section 6.5 states the Pool "is therefore likely to close at the end of the 2025/26 financial year." Historically this has generated substantial bonuses: £1,050,924 (2024/25), £928,265 (2022/23), £570,894 (2023/24). This income has been moved into earmarked reserves to fund future budget gaps; the loss removes both future bonus income and undermines the strategy of building reserves to absorb MTFS pressures.
findings.matters: A material recurring income stream the council has relied on to bolster reserves is ending; combined with LGR costs and investment income decline, this compounds revenue pressure.
findings.quote: The reset of the Business Rates system takes the Council back to a new Baseline and will effectively take out the growth over baseline achieved over the last decade that has made it beneficial to be a member of the Business Rates Pool. The Pool is therefore likely to close at the end of the 2025/26 financial year.

findings.paper_title: Budget Paper for February Council - with final settlement figures
findings.headline: Investment income cliff: £625,889 above-budget returns in 2024/25 will disappear as interest rates fall, eroding revenue assumptions
findings.detail: The council received £625,889 above budget from treasury management short-term investing in 2024/25, and is forecasting similar returns in 2025/26. The MTFS for 2026/27 holds investment income at the same level (matching 2025/26), but section 5.2 explicitly flags this: "As interest rates fall back, so do these income returns." Section 7.8 states "as interest rates fall, we will no longer benefit from this additional income." This represents £600k+ of budget assumptions resting on returns that are already declining.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council's balanced budget depends on income that is structurally falling, not cyclical; this will force either service cuts or further reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: £625,889 above-budget returns 2024/25; investment income base budget held flat 2026/27 despite falling rates
findings.quote: As interest rates fall, we will no longer benefit from this additional income and so the base budget for investment income in 2026/27 will be kept as is.

findings.paper_title: Budget Paper for February Council - with final settlement figures
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation transformation costs unquantified but flagged as material and likely to impact reserves in years 2-3
findings.detail: The council has earmarked £1m for LGR costs and budgeted Project Office costs for 2026/27, but explicitly states that transformation costs (redundancies and pension strain) cannot yet be estimated. Section 3.10 warns these "are likely to be material amounts which will impact the MTFS in years 2 and 3." The budget notes this is a significant unknown that will only be clarified when government announces the successful bid outcome in summer 2026, with vesting day 1 April 2028.
findings.matters: Material unquantified liabilities alongside an already-tight MTFS in years 2-3 create a significant risk profile for repayment capacity; a three-year view is insufficient for a council facing structural reorganisation.
findings.figures: £1m earmarked reserve for LGR; unquantified redundancy and pension strain costs flagged as material
findings.quote: The transformation costs of LGR i.e. any redundancies and the associated pension strain cannot be estimated at this time, but they are likely to be material amounts which will impact the MTFS in years 2 and 3.

findings.paper_title: Budget Paper for February Council - with final settlement figures
findings.headline: Funding settlement methodology change removes £2.3m from years 2-3 MTFS, requiring reserve drawdown to balance
findings.detail: The final settlement changed Business Rates pooling from 100% to the district to a 50/50 split with the County. For 2026/27 an Adjustment Support Grant protects the council (£1,053,102), but comparing provisional to final settlement figures shows a net reduction in central government funding of £2,318,502 in years 2 and 3. This will force increased reliance on reserves to balance the budget in 2027/28 and 2028/29.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether a council's future solvency rests on ongoing reserves rather than sustainable revenue, and whether organisational changes could disrupt this strategy.
findings.figures: £2,318,502 net reduction in central government funding years 2-3; £1,053,102 Adjustment Support Grant for 2026/27 only
findings.quote: The reduction in funding in future years will require the increased use of reserves to balance the revenue budget in 2027/28 and 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: Report of the Chief Finance Officer on the 202627 Budget FINAL
findings.headline: Investment property income is volatile and material to front-line services funding
findings.detail: The council explicitly identifies investment property income as a vital revenue stream, but one that is volatile. They have mitigated this by setting up an Investment Property Reserve, bringing the Property and Assets team back in-house from Publica, and developing an Asset Management Strategy.
findings.matters: A volatile income stream that funds front-line services creates budget risk. A market downturn or major tenant failure would create a gap. The council is managing the risk but the vulnerability remains.
findings.figures: Investment property income identified as vital to funding front-line services; mitigated by reserve and strategy
findings.quote: Investment Property income is a vital revenue stream to fund front line Council services. The income can be volatile and is therefore another key risk for the Council.

findings.paper_title: Report of the Chief Finance Officer on the 202627 Budget FINAL
findings.headline: Treasury management income is falling as interest rates decline after exceptional returns
findings.detail: Over recent years, the council's cash management has generated income returns far higher than budget due to high interest rates and returns from Money Market Funds and DMO investments. As interest rates fall back, these income returns will decline materially. The council budgeted conservatively, so this is a headwind to the balance.
findings.matters: A significant income source that has helped balance the budget is now reversing. The council will need to identify other income sources or make savings to offset the decline.
findings.figures: Interest rates slowly starting to come down; income returns from MMF and DMO have been exceptionally high but will fall
findings.quote: Over recent years Treasury Management short term investing has produced income returns far higher than budget due to prevailing global economic conditions and the high rate of return from the Money Market Funds (MMF) and Debt Management Office (DMO). As interest rates fall back, so do these income returns.

findings.paper_title: Report of the Chief Finance Officer on the 202627 Budget FINAL
findings.headline: Leisure contract income is material and at risk: current contract ends 2027, extension negotiations ongoing
findings.detail: The existing leisure contract with Greenwich Leisure Limited returns significant income to the council and ends in 2027. In October 2025 the Executive agreed to negotiate a five-year extension and delegated authority to the Director of Place. The estimated impact of the negotiation is built into the MTFS, but the outcome is not yet certain.
findings.matters: A material income stream is in play. If negotiations fail or produce worse terms, the council will face a budget gap mid-MTFS. Delegated authority means council has limited oversight until a deal is done.
findings.figures: Contract ends 2027; extension negotiations delegated to Director of Place with others in consultation
findings.quote: The existing leisure contract, which comes to an end in 2027, returns a significant level of income to the Council. In October 2025, the Executive agreed to enter a five-year contract extension with Greenwich Leisure Limited (GLL).

findings.paper_title: Report of the Chief Finance Officer on the 202627 Budget FINAL
findings.headline: If LGR is delayed, the council may need to implement a savings programme to balance the budget
findings.detail: The CFO states that the medium-term financial strategy assumes the council will continue to operate as usual, but if LGR is delayed, reserves depletion will force contingent savings. The general fund balance is already declining over the life of the MTFS despite being 'relatively healthy' now.
findings.matters: A contingent savings requirement means the council has no agreed plan for that scenario and would need to act quickly if triggered. Unplanned service cuts carry execution risk.
findings.figures: General fund balance reducing over the life of MTFS; expected contribution to reserves in 2026/27 is £683,814 before growth
findings.quote: If LGR were to be delayed for any reason, the Council may need to implement a savings programme in order to continue to produce a balanced budget past the life of the current MTFS.

findings.paper_title: Report of the Chief Finance Officer on the 202627 Budget FINAL
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation will materially impact reserves before 2028, timing and cost unknown
findings.detail: The council cannot produce credible financial projections until the government confirms its LGR decision, expected summer 2026. The CFO explicitly warns that transformation costs are a significant unknown and will undoubtedly require substantial resources, with material impact on the MTFS in years 2 and 3. They have set up an Earmarked Reserve to fund LGR costs, but this will reduce the council's financial cushion.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council can absorb a major structural transformation without breaching covenants or reserve adequacy. The timing uncertainty and unquantified cost creates medium-term debt servicing risk.
findings.figures: Decision expected summer 2026; costs will impact MTFS in years 2 and 3; council expects to hold general fund balances of just under £12.55m at end of this year
findings.quote: A significant unknown at present is the transformation costs of LGR. It would be prudent to assume that there will be a significant impact on General Fund reserves before 2028.

findings.headline: Waste vehicle fleet replacement delayed to Q4 2026/27 due to supply chain constraints; 4 electric food waste vehicles on extended lead time
findings.detail: A phased waste vehicle replacement programme approved February 2024 includes 4 electric food waste vehicles now on order with delivery estimated Q4 2026/27 due to supply chain lead times. This delays critical service infrastructure renewal and creates risk that shortages or cost escalations could require expedited procurement.
findings.matters: Infrastructure delivery delays, particularly for waste fleet, indicate supply-side constraints that could force cost escalations or service disruptions if the council cannot absorb delays.
findings.figures: 4 electric food waste vehicles ordered, delivery Q4 2026/27. 2 standard fuel vehicles and 3 electric supervisor vans already delivered (Sept 2024, Feb 2025).
findings.quote: The 4 electric food waste vehicles are on order with a delivery time estimated as Q4 2026/27 due to long lead times in the supply chain.

findings.headline: Net revenue stream declining 30% over four years (£16.43m to £11.41m by 2029/30) while financing costs as % of revenue rise to 10.20%
findings.detail: The council's net revenue stream (Council Tax, business rates, grants) declines from £16.43m in 2026/27 to £11.41m in 2029/30. Simultaneously, financing costs as a percentage of that shrinking revenue base rise from 5.26% (2026/27) to 10.20% (2029/30). This squeeze—shrinking income combined with rising debt servicing costs—reduces headroom for unexpected pressures.
findings.matters: A declining income base combined with rising financing costs signals potential revenue stress. The council's ability to absorb service cost pressures or income volatility becomes materially constrained.
findings.quote: the ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream is very low and meet the requirements to be affordable and proportionate.

findings.headline: Reserve drawdown: 50% of investment property repairs funded from earmarked reserves rather than external contributions, depleting capital cushion
findings.detail: The capital financing table shows earmarked reserves funding 50% of investment property repair costs in 2026/27, with internal borrowing funding the remainder. This includes the significant Carterton Industrial Estate re-roofing project. Reserve depletion for asset maintenance rather than reserve accumulation suggests capital constraints when investment income is increasingly critical to the budget.
findings.matters: Depleting earmarked reserves to maintain asset condition (especially income-generating property) reduces financial headroom at a time when investment income is increasingly important to the revenue budget.
findings.figures: 50% of 2026/27 investment property repairs from earmarked reserves. Carterton re-roofing project £0.5m funded partly from reserves, completion expected spring 2026.
findings.quote: Earmarked Reserves – during 2026/27 50% of the repairs to Investment Properties will be funded through earmarked reserves with the remainder through internal borrowing.

findings.headline: Capital projects creating new ongoing revenue cost obligations: decarbonisation work requires £565,000 council contribution plus ongoing maintenance costs
findings.detail: Witney Leisure Centre decarbonisation secured grant funding from SALIX but grant does not cover full cost. The council must contribute approximately £565,000 as capital and fund ongoing revenue costs for the thermal systems. This creates a fixed ongoing revenue burden from a capital project, reducing budget flexibility.
findings.matters: Capital schemes that generate ongoing revenue cost obligations reduce financial flexibility and should factor into affordability assessments, particularly when net revenue stream is declining.
findings.figures: £565,000 council contribution to decarbonisation, plus unquantified ongoing revenue costs.
findings.quote: Grant funding will not cover the entire cost of the decarbonisation project. The Council will have to make an estimated contribution of £565,000 as well as fund ongoing revenue costs.

findings.headline: Acute temporary accommodation crisis: 80 people in need against 24 available units, requiring £3m capital acquisition with delayed legal completion
findings.detail: The council identified in 2025/26 that 80 people required emergency accommodation but only had 24 units available. It allocated £3m to acquire 30 additional beds. As of February 2026, only one property had completed (November 2025) and legal work was still in progress on further acquisitions, with no occupation date available. The properties will require refurbishment.
findings.matters: Demand-driven capital spend with extended delivery timeline creates risk of cost overruns and ongoing pressure if homelessness demand grows faster than acquisition pace can address.
findings.figures: 80 people in need, 24 available units, 29 beds identified for acquisition, £3m allocated, 1 property completed as of Nov 2025.
findings.quote: The need for Temporary Emergency Accommodation was recognised as acute in 2025/26, with an average of 80 people in need of accommodation but the Council only having 24 units available.

findings.headline: Investment property income rising to 38% of net revenue by 2028/29, while PWLB rules prevent reinvestment in yield-generating replacement assets
findings.detail: Investment income (capital and service combined) is projected at 28.44% of net revenue stream in 2026/27, rising to 38.19% by 2028/29. The council explicitly states that current PWLB rules prevent it from purchasing replacement income-generating assets, creating a mismatch between growing reliance on property income and inability to renew or replace that income base if tenancies end or property values fall.
findings.matters: A lender must assess the council's vulnerability to loss of this income stream. Growing structural dependence on property rental income combined with inability to invest receipts in replacement yields creates concentration risk.
findings.figures: Investment income 28.44% of net revenue (2026/27), rising to 38.19% (2028/29). Capital investments £3.10m, service investments £1.13m (2026/27).
findings.quote: Large scale sale of our investment property portfolio is not recommended with the current PWLB rules not permitting the Council to purchase replacement assets for yield.

findings.paper_title: Annex L - Treasury Management Strategy 2627 FINAL
findings.headline: Statutory override protecting pooled fund losses from revenue budget expires 31 March 2029; losses may then impact revenue accounts.
findings.detail: A temporary statutory override allows fair value gains and losses on pooled funds to be recorded in an unusable reserve rather than hitting the revenue account (unless the fund is sold). The council extended this override to 31 March 2029 for investments held before 1 April 2024. After this date, if pooled funds have not recovered capital value, losses will impact the revenue budget.
findings.matters: The override is a temporary protection masking the true revenue impact of investment losses. A lender needs to understand when this accounting protection expires and what the exposure is if capital recovery does not materialise.
findings.figures: Override expires 31 March 2029, applies to investments held before 1 April 2024
findings.quote: The statutory override for pooled funds, which allows fair value gains and losses to be recorded in an unusable reserve rather than the revenue account (unless the fund is sold), has been extended until 31 March 2029 for investments held before 1 April 2024.

findings.paper_title: Annex L - Treasury Management Strategy 2627 FINAL
findings.headline: Council revenue budget relies on investment income from volatile pooled funds; investment income is a 'vital income stream' to support the budget.
findings.detail: The council holds £35.47m in investments (as of 31 December 2025), with £12.47m in strategic pooled funds generating 4.36% annualised income return. The council explicitly states that investment income is a vital income stream supporting the revenue budget. Some pooled funds show volatile returns (Schroder Income Maximiser at 23.25% one-year return, but Fundamentum Social Housing REIT at -2.54%).
findings.matters: If market conditions deteriorate or investment returns fall sharply, the council's revenue budget is exposed. A lender needs to understand the degree to which spending plans depend on investment market conditions.
findings.figures: £35.47m total investments (Dec 2025), £12.47m in pooled funds, annualised income return 4.36% (pooled), 4.14% (overall)
findings.quote: The Council has cash balances invested in various financial instruments; Money Market Funds, Short Term deposits and pooled funds, delivering a vital income stream to support the Council's revenue budget.

findings.paper_title: Annex L - Treasury Management Strategy 2627 FINAL
findings.headline: Pooled fund investments have already suffered material capital losses; council used earmarked reserve to absorb UBS fund withdrawal in September 2024.
findings.detail: Over the last three years, the council's pooled funds lost significant capital value. In September 2024, the UBS pooled fund was withdrawn and losses were covered by an earmarked reserve established in 2023/24. Treasury advisors forecast complete capital recovery over the next 18-24 months as interest rates fall, but this assumption underpins the strategy.
findings.matters: A lender assessing financial resilience needs to know the council has already absorbed pooled fund losses and the degree to which future capital recovery assumptions are critical to the financial plan.
findings.figures: UBS pooled fund withdrawal September 2024, remaining reserve balance to be released
findings.quote: Events in the financial markets in the last three years have meant that many of our pooled funds lost a material amount of capital value while producing a significantly higher revenue return. The capital value has significantly recovered over the last year with current advice from our Treasury advisors being a complete recovery over the next 18 months to 2 years as interest rates fall.

findings.paper_title: Annex L - Treasury Management Strategy 2627 FINAL
findings.headline: Council will enter external borrowing before end of 2027/28 to fund capital expenditure, shifting from current debt-free position.
findings.detail: The council is transitioning from internal borrowing (using cash reserves) to external borrowing to fund capital programs including waste vehicle fleet replacement. External borrowing is forecast at £2.75m in 2027/28, £2.55m in 2028/29, and £2.16m in 2029/30. The Capital Financing Requirement (CFR) is £33.46m for 2026/27, declining as the capital program is completed.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand when the council will enter the debt market and the scale of future borrowing requirements. This is the first external debt after an extended debt-free period.
findings.quote: The Council is likely to enter into debt before the end of 2027/28 to fund the replacement of the waste vehicle fleet and other planned capital expenditure which is demonstrated by the table above.

findings.headline: Investment property portfolio remains essential to revenue budget despite PWLB restrictions on yield-focused investments.
findings.detail: The council holds £53.49m of investment property (commercial and industrial) that generates £3.104m annual return forecast for 2026/27. The document states: 'With the PWLB's restrictions on allowable investments, the existing property portfolio is extremely valuable to the Council.' If the portfolio is sold, the council cannot replace that income stream because yield-focused investments are now ineligible for PWLB borrowing.
findings.matters: The council is locked into holding an illiquid, concentrated property portfolio because it has no other way to generate the income it needs; this reduces financial flexibility and increases concentration risk.
findings.figures: Property investment value £53.49m; forecast return 2026/27: £3.104m; represents 70% of total investment income forecast
findings.quote: With the PWLB's restrictions on allowable investments, the existing property portfolio is extremely valuable to the Council.

findings.headline: Vacant Between Towns Road office building is in process of being sold to fund capital programme.
findings.detail: The council is selling a vacant office building to generate capital receipt for the capital programme, reducing future external borrowing needs. This reflects post-pandemic decline in demand for office space.
findings.matters: Asset sales to fund capital spending indicate either cash pressure or strategic repositioning; loss of office building may also reduce future rental income.
findings.figures: Not quantified; property portfolio value as at 31 March 2025 is £53.49m total (£25.61m inside district, £27.88m outside)
findings.quote: The Council's vacant office building at Between Towns Road is in the process of being sold with the resulting capital receipt being used to deliver the capital programme thereby reducing the amount of any future external borrowing.

findings.headline: Council plans to borrow in 2026/27 to part-finance replacement of waste vehicle fleet.
findings.detail: The council states it has plans to borrow to finance replacement of the waste fleet in 2026/27. This is a new borrowing commitment and will increase the council's debt servicing costs from 2026/27 onwards.
findings.matters: New borrowing increases debt and debt-servicing costs; timing and size affect the council's financial headroom over the MTFS.
findings.figures: Not quantified in the document; described as 'part finance' so likely a material but not full replacement cost
findings.quote: The Council has plans to borrow in 2026/27 to part finance the replacement of the waste vehicle fleet but has no plans to borrow in advance of need.

findings.headline: Usable reserves forecast to decline from £33.42m to £13.73m over the MTFS period (2026/27 to 2029/30).
findings.detail: The council's usable reserves are forecast to decline by approximately £19.7m over four years, falling from £33.42m in 2026/27 to £13.73m by 2029/30. This is driven by the cash funding forecasts and implies ongoing reliance on reserves to bridge budget gaps.
findings.matters: Declining reserves reduce a council's buffer against unexpected costs and signal potential financial stress; lenders monitor reserve coverage closely.

findings.headline: Total investment income as a share of council spending falls from 18.44% to 12.77% in one year, reducing revenue funding flexibility.
findings.detail: The council's investment income (treasury, loans, and property combined) is forecast to drop from £6.28m (18.44% of service spending) in 2025/26 to £4.43m (12.77%) in 2026/27 and stay at that lower level. The document warns: 'If it cannot generate sufficient income to fund its budget, the Council will be required to draw additional balances from reserves or generate savings elsewhere within the budget.'
findings.matters: A council that relies on investment income for over 12% of its budget faces budget stress if returns fall short of forecast; this is a key vulnerability lenders assess.
findings.figures: 2025/26 total £6.28m (18.44% of £34.04m expenditure); 2026/27 forecast £4.43m (12.77% of £34.72m expenditure)
findings.quote: If it cannot generate sufficient income to fund its budget, the Council will be required to draw additional balances from reserves or generate savings elsewhere within the budget to continue to provide its services.

findings.headline: Treasury investment income forecast drops to zero from 2026/27 onwards, after earning £1.84m in 2025/26.
findings.detail: The council's short-term and medium-term treasury investments are forecast to generate no revenue return from 2026/27 onwards, a dramatic shift from the £1.84m earned in 2025/26. This is attributed to expected falls in interest rates. Treasury income is currently one of the main income streams supporting the revenue budget.
findings.matters: A sudden loss of £1.8m in forecast annual revenue is material; if not offset by other income, it forces either reserve drawdown or service cuts.
findings.figures: 2025/26 actual £1.84m; 2026/27 forecast £0.00m; 2027/28-2029/30 forecast £0.00m each year
findings.quote: Treasury Investment Income 1.84 0.00 0.00 0.00 0.00

findings.headline: Increasing annual reliance on General Fund reserve drawdowns to balance budgets, rising to £2.4m by 2029/30
findings.detail: The council is drawing from reserves every year from 2026/27 onwards to balance the budget, with draws rising from £348k to £2.36m annually. This is unsustainable without action—it implies budgeted spending exceeds income.
findings.matters: Drawing reserves annually to meet spending is a warning signal. Once reserves are exhausted, the council will be forced to cut services, borrow, or trigger intervention.

findings.headline: Revenue Support Grant collapses from £7.5m to £275k by 2029/30, removing structural government support
findings.detail: RSG falls by 96% over five years, from £7.5m in 2025/26 to £274k by 2029/30. The council must backfill this loss through savings, reserves, or increasing Council Tax and other income.
findings.matters: RSG withdrawal is a structural change, not a cycle. If reserves are depleted before alternatives are secured, the council faces difficult choices about service cuts or borrowing.

findings.headline: General Fund reserves projected to fall 41% over five years, from £12.6m to £7.4m
findings.detail: The council's reserves decline by £5.2m between 2025/26 and 2029/30. The drawdown accelerates from 2027/28 onwards: £824k in 2027/28, £1.67m in 2028/29, and £2.36m in 2029/30. This trajectory suggests structural overspend.
findings.matters: Lenders rely on reserves as a buffer against shocks and evidence of prudent management. Reserves below £7m limit the council's ability to absorb spending pressures or income shortfalls.

findings.headline: Extended Producer Responsibility (Waste) funding of £2.99m ends entirely in 2026/27
findings.detail: The council loses a £2.99m government grant in 2026/27 with no compensation shown in the plan. This is roughly 17% of the general fund balance and requires either savings, tax rises, or reserve drawdowns to offset.
findings.matters: An unexpected loss of nearly £3m in a single year is material to affordability and the council's headroom.
findings.quote: Extended Producer Responsibility (Waste) (2,990,216) 0 0 0 0

findings.paper_title: Annex A - MTFS Draft for January Meetings
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation funding of £350k and £650k allocated for first two years, signalling structural governance changes.
findings.detail: The MTFS includes significant one-off spending allocations for local government reorganisation: £350k in 2026/27 and £650k in 2027/28. This indicates the council expects structural changes to its governance or service delivery during this period.
findings.matters: Restructuring introduces execution risk and transition costs. A lender needs visibility on what changes are planned, their cost, and whether they will improve or worsen the council's medium-term financial position.
findings.figures: Local Government Reorganisation spending: £350,000 (2026/27) and £650,000 (2027/28)
findings.quote: Local Government Re-Organisation 350,000 650,000

findings.paper_title: Annex A - MTFS Draft for January Meetings
findings.headline: Service cuts and asset disposals underway, including closure of public conveniences and sale of Between Towns Road property.
findings.detail: The budget incorporates discrete cost-reduction measures: £100k from closure of some public conveniences, and a one-off asset disposal at Between Towns Road (£157.8k). These are concrete service reductions and capital disposals required to balance the budget.
findings.matters: Service cuts and forced asset sales indicate financial strain is driving operational decisions, not strategy. Together with reserve depletion and council tax rises, they suggest a council under sustained financial pressure.
findings.figures: Public convenience closure saving: £100,000; Between Towns Road disposal: £157,826
findings.quote: Closure of some Public Conveniences(100,000) ... Disposal of Between Towns Road(157,826)

findings.paper_title: Annex A - MTFS Draft for January Meetings
findings.headline: Council tax must increase 3.5–3.9% annually every year to cover the budget gap from central government funding withdrawal.
findings.detail: The MTFS projects consecutive years of council tax increases at 3.86%, 3.72%, 3.59%, 3.46%, and 3.35% from 2026/27 through 2030/31. These sustained above-inflation increases, each year without break, indicate the council's dependency on raising the tax burden to compensate for lost government support rather than achieving underlying budget balance.
findings.matters: Persistent council tax increases at this level can trigger resident pushback, limit collection rates, and signal a council unable to balance its structural position without transferring pressure to taxpayers.

findings.paper_title: Annex A - MTFS Draft for January Meetings
findings.headline: Revenue Support Grant funding disappears almost entirely, collapsing from £7.5m to £275k—a 96% reduction in core government funding.
findings.detail: Government revenue support drops precipitously: from £7.52m in 2026/27 to £5.22m in 2027/28, then £2.85m, £550k, and finally £275k by 2030/31. This cliff-edge loss is partially cushioned by an Income Protection Floor (transitional funding reaching £5.34m in 2029/30), but that protection itself reduces by £1.25m when it expires after 2029/30. The council faces a structural funding crisis requiring sustained council tax rises and service reductions.
findings.matters: A lender needs certainty about structural funding. A council losing nearly all government grant revenue whilst depending on a transitional protection mechanism that itself expires represents significant medium-term financial risk.
findings.figures: Revenue Support Grant: 7,522,982 (2026/27) to 274,828 (2030/31); Income Protection Floor: 776,198 to 5,343,995 to 4,093,995 (drops by £1.25m in 2030/31)

findings.paper_title: Annex A - MTFS Draft for January Meetings
findings.headline: General fund reserves decline from £12.6m to £3m by 2030/31, with accelerating annual drawdowns in later years.
findings.detail: West Oxfordshire's general fund balance is projected to fall from £12.56m in 2026/27 to £2.95m by 2030/31. While reserves are added in the first year (£650k), subsequent years show escalating drawdowns: £538k in 2027/28 growing to £3.59m annually by 2030/31. This trajectory leaves the council with minimal financial buffers to absorb unexpected pressures or further shortfalls.
findings.matters: A lender relies on council reserves as a backstop against financial stress. Reserves depleted to 13% of annual budget in five years signal rising financial vulnerability and reduced capacity to manage volatility.
findings.figures: General fund balance declining from 12,557,909 to 2,951,763; use of GF reserves growing from 538,532 (2027/28) to 3,593,679 (2030/31)

findings.headline: Investment income is declining by 18% over five years, from £1.16m to £0.95m.
findings.detail: Pooled fund investment income falls from £1,156,227 in 2026/27 to £949,427 by 2030/31. This reflects declining interest rate assumptions and erodes a secondary but material income source.
findings.matters: A lender would note that the council's income base is shrinking across multiple sources simultaneously—government grants, investment returns—forcing heavier reliance on council tax and reserves.
findings.figures: Investment income: £1,156,227 → £949,427 (decline of £206,800)

findings.headline: New temporary accommodation commitment introduced with £28,212 budget allocation.
findings.detail: Temporary accommodation appears as a new line in the MTFS, indicating the council has taken on a new or expanded service. This typically reflects homelessness or housing pressure and often grows beyond initial forecasts.
findings.matters: New statutory or quasi-statutory commitments are often early signals of emerging service pressures. Temporary accommodation budgets have historically underestimated demand in many councils.
findings.quote: New Temporary Accommodation(28,212)

findings.headline: Council tax is rising 3.8–3.9% annually, with the band D charge increasing from £134.38 to £154.38 (15% cumulative).
findings.detail: Annual increases begin at 3.86% and decline only slightly to 3.35% by 2030/31, well above the inflation assumptions in the plan itself (2–2.5%). This suggests council tax is being used to partially plug the government funding gap.
findings.matters: Large and sustained council tax increases signal that residents are bearing an increasing burden and may face political resistance or affordability limits. A lender would note this as a constraint on the council's ability to raise further revenue.
findings.figures: Band D: £134.38 → £154.38 (15% rise); annual tax increases: 3.86% → 3.35%

findings.headline: Government funding is halving over five years, from £6.4m to £3.9m in Revenue Support Grant alone.
findings.detail: The council's Revenue Support Grant will fall 39% in five years. Combined with business rates income, total government grants and business rates funding falls from £12.05m to £6.77m. This cliff is the primary driver of reserve depletion.
findings.matters: Loss of major income sources forces councils to either cut services, raise council tax, or draw reserves. West Oxfordshire is doing all three. A lender evaluating credit risk would note whether the council can manage this without financial distress.
findings.figures: Revenue Support Grant: £6,400,150 → £3,911,886 (39% decline); Total government grants and business rates: £12,053,342 → £6,769,402

findings.headline: Council will draw down reserves at an accelerating rate, reaching £3.6m by 2030/31.
findings.detail: General fund reserves usage rises from £21,448 in 2026/27 to £3.5m by year five. This is not a one-off; the trajectory worsens year on year, indicating the budget cannot be balanced from sustainable income. By 2030/31, reserves are being used to cover 17% of the gap between controllable spending and core funding.
findings.matters: Accelerating reserve drawdown exhaust financial resilience and signals structural imbalance. A lender assesses whether a council can service debt from operating cash, not from the reserve pool.

findings.headline: Council tax rises required every year at 3.86%, 3.72%, 3.59%, 3.46%, 3.35%
findings.detail: To balance the budget without deeper reserve drawdown, the council is planning above-inflation council tax increases every single year. Band D rises from £134.38 to £154.38. The trajectory suggests sustained inability to match spending to permanent revenue.
findings.matters: Persistent above-inflation rises signal financial stress and risk pushback from residents. They are unsustainable beyond two or three years without service cuts.
findings.figures: Band D: 134.38 (2026/27) to 154.38 (2030/31); Tax increase: 3.86% declining to 3.35%

findings.headline: Revenue Support Grant falls 40% in three years, from £6.4m to £3.7m
findings.detail: The council's central government revenue support grant drops from £6.4m in 2026/27 to £5.0m in 2027/28, then to £3.7m by 2028/29. This is a cliff, not a gradual reduction. The council is budgeting for this but offering no narrative on how it manages the step change.
findings.matters: A sudden 40% loss of core government funding forces difficult cuts. The narrative should explain what services are at risk or what reserves are being used to bridge it.

findings.headline: General fund balance falls from £12.6m to £1.1m—a 91% depletion over five years
findings.detail: Starting position is £12.6m in 2026/27. By 2030/31 it is down to £1.1m. The council is drawing down reserves by £1.7m to £3.2m per year from 2027/28 onward to balance its books. A fund balance of £1.1m at the end is materially tight.
findings.matters: Rapidly depleting reserves indicate the council cannot fund its budget from permanent revenue. A fund balance of £1.1m leaves no buffer for shocks or slippage.
findings.figures: General fund balance: 12,557,909 (2026/27) declining to 1,139,083 (2030/31)

findings.headline: Extended Producer Responsibility grant of £2.99m in 2026/27 then vanishes entirely
findings.detail: The council receives a one-off waste grant of nearly £3m in year one only. This disappears completely from 2027/28 onward, leaving a £3m hole in future years' income. Without identifying this gap explicitly in the narrative, the budget could disguise a structural deficit.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council can live within its permanent revenue. A £3m temporary income stream masks the true underlying position.
findings.figures: Extended Producer Responsibility (Waste): (2,990,216) 2026/27, then 0 for all following years
findings.quote: Extended Producer Responsibility (Waste) (2,990,216) 0 0 0 0

findings.headline: Waste contract (Ubico) ends March 2027 with no further extensions available; collaborative options under development
findings.detail: The Ubico waste contract, whose costs have been rising over recent years, is extended only to March 2027 with potential variation from April 2026. No further extensions are available beyond that date. In January 2025, the Executive resolved to work with other Oxfordshire authorities on a collaborative waste and environmental services transformation programme, but options are still being developed.
findings.matters: A major council service contract ends in 15 months with no agreed successor arrangement, creating service continuity and pricing uncertainty.
findings.figures: Contract ends March 2027; variation option from April 2026
findings.quote: The Ubico waste contract, the costs of which have been rising over recent years, saw a modest saving in the 2025/26 budget setting process, The contract was extended to March 2027, with the potential to vary from April 2026, with no further extensions available after this date.

findings.headline: General Fund reserves are adequate but 'not infinite' to cover medium-term budget gaps identified in the MTFS
findings.detail: The council states it has adequate reserves in the medium term to fill the MTFS gap, but adds a critical caveat: 'these reserves are not infinite'. The MTFS identifies funding pressures including the £3m Business Rates Reset loss, leisure contract income loss from 2027, and inflationary cost pressures. Reserves are being eroded over time to balance the budget.
findings.matters: The council is dependent on running down reserves to cover recurring revenue shortfalls; this is not sustainable and reserves will eventually be exhausted unless spending or income improves.
findings.figures: Net assets increased to £154.71m in 2024/25; total usable reserves £47.36m
findings.quote: With careful financial management and doing the best possible in terms of the factors within our control, the Council has adequate reserves to fill the gap in the revenue budget identified in the MTFS in the medium term. However, these reserves are not infinite and there are a few key challenges ahead for us as a district council.

findings.headline: 2024/25 outturn surplus of £6,345 driven by one-off items that 'cannot be relied upon on an ongoing basis'
findings.detail: After Q1 forecast a significant overspend and Q3 still forecast £34,344 overspend, the council achieved a final surplus of £6,345. The finance narrative explicitly warns this was due to 'one-off beneficial variances' including treasury investment income, reduced capital spend and below-budget MRP and grants, and 'these events cannot be relied upon on an ongoing basis'.
findings.matters: The council's apparent financial improvement is temporary and masks an underlying structural budget gap that is being papered over. Future years will not have these windfalls.
findings.figures: 2024/25 outturn surplus £6,345; Q1 forecast significant overspend; Q3 forecast £34,344 overspend
findings.quote: These events cannot be relied upon on an ongoing basis.

findings.headline: Carterton Industrial Estate units vacant pending roof repairs, impacting investment property performance
findings.detail: Three units at Carterton Industrial Estate are vacant because roof repairs are required before they can be let. The tender process for repairs is complete and work is 'anticipated to start imminently'. This estate is part of the council's investment property portfolio which showed mixed year-on-year performance.
findings.matters: A capital asset central to the council's property investment income is out of commission and generating no rental income until repairs are complete.
findings.figures: Three units vacant; overall investment portfolio showed £29,597 underspend excluding this estate
findings.quote: Carterton Industrial Estate (Units 1-3) showed an overspend as they are vacant as repairs to the roof are required before the units can be tenanted. The tender process for this work is now complete and work is anticipated to start imminently.

findings.headline: Business Rates collection fund deficit of £0.155m in 2024/25 rolled into 2025/26 budget via earmarked reserves
findings.detail: The council has a £0.155m deficit on retained business rates income for 2024/25 caused by government extensions of retail, leisure and hospitality reliefs. The corresponding Section 31 compensation grant has been moved to earmarked reserves to cover the repayment of the deficit in 2025/26.
findings.matters: A recurring collection fund deficit signals sustained pressure on the council's core tax/rates income and dependence on government compensation.
findings.quote: There is a £0.155m deficit in our retained Business Rate income for 2024/25 due to the extension of government reliefs to the Retail, Leisure and Hospitality Sectors.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation will end the council on 31 March 2028, creating major organisational challenge
findings.detail: Following the English Devolution White Paper (December 2024), West Oxfordshire will cease to exist as a council on 31 March 2028 and merge into a new unitary authority from 1 April 2028. Three options are being developed, with government decision expected in late 2025. Elections to shadow authorities are scheduled for April/May 2027.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand that the council will not exist in its current form after 2028, there is significant organisational uncertainty for the next two years, and any long-term commitments or borrowing must account for this structural change.
findings.figures: Vesting day: 1 April 2028; shadow authority elections April/May 2027
findings.quote: This would mean that West Oxfordshire District Council would cease to be a Council on 31 March 2028, and would be merged into a new Unitary Council as from 1 April 2028, referred to as the vesting day.

findings.headline: Business Rates Reset in 2026 will cost the council £3m in lost funding, built into the MTFS
findings.detail: The Medium Term Financial Strategy already recognises an expected loss of £3m funding through the Business Rates Reset in 2026. This is treated as a settled part of the funding challenge to be filled by reserves drawdown.
findings.matters: A £3m annual loss is material for a district council and is being managed by drawing down general fund reserves, reducing financial resilience.
findings.figures: £3m loss expected in 2026
findings.quote: The expected loss of £3m of funding through the Business Rates Reset in 2026.

findings.headline: Fair Funding Review expected to have material negative impact on funding, with magnitude dependent on government compensation
findings.detail: The council has 'benefitted disproportionately from business rates' and the Fair Funding Review 2.0 (consultation closes 15 August 2025) will reset the business rates retention system. The council states a material negative impact is expected, but the size depends on compensation funding from government. Changes are proposed to be phased in from 2026/27.
findings.matters: A material adverse impact on funding is locked in but unknowable until the government decides on compensation levels, leaving the council unable to fully forecast its medium-term position.
findings.figures: Implementation begins 2026/27, phased over three years
findings.quote: West Oxfordshire has benefitted disproportionately from business rates and therefore a reset is expected to have a material impact on funding levels. The size of the impact will depend on the level of compensation funding provided by the government. The proposed changes will be implemented over three years, beginning in 2026-27.

findings.headline: Leisure contract expires in 2027 with material impact on funding strategy acknowledged but unquantified
findings.detail: The Greenwich Leisure Limited contract expires in 2027. The council is conducting an options appraisal but states explicitly that whatever outcome is chosen, the impact on the Medium Term Financial Strategy will be material and presents 'a significant challenge ahead'. No figures provided for the scale of the impact.
findings.matters: A loss of leisure contract income in 2027 is a known, material funding gap within the MTFS planning horizon, and the council acknowledges it has no solution yet.
findings.figures: Contract expires 2027; material impact flagged but not quantified
findings.quote: The current leisure contract with GLL expires in 2027, and an options appraisal is underway to determine the best course of action for the Council in terms of a contract from 2027. Whatever the outcome of this piece of work, there is going to be a material impact on the Medium-Term Financial Strategy (MTFS) in 2027 which presents a significant challenge ahead.

findings.paper_title: A WODC FY25 Audit Completion Report
findings.headline: Pension fund deficit of £3.91m, down from £4.97m but driven entirely by discount rate movement rather than funding improvements
findings.detail: The council's net pension liability decreased by £1.06m year-on-year from £4.97m to £3.91m. However, the auditor explicitly notes this was driven by an increase in the discount rate from 4.80% to 5.80%, which mechanically reduces the present value of future liabilities rather than indicating improved funding or contribution position. The unfunded obligations liability remains at £0.40m. The recognised liability under IFRS is £3.51m after applying the asset ceiling rule.
findings.matters: The pension deficit remains a material balance sheet liability; while it improved, this was due to market interest rate movements, not council actions or funding progress, so the underlying financial commitment remains substantial.
findings.figures: Deficit 2024/25: £3.91m; 2023/24: £4.97m; discount rate increase from 4.80% to 5.80%; unfunded obligations £0.40m; recognised liability £3.51m
findings.quote: The pension valuation has moved from a net deficit of £4.97m at 31 March 2024 to a net deficit position of £3.91m at 31 March 2025. This is inclusive of the liability for unfunded obligations of £0.40m (2023/24: £0.44m). The key driver of that change was the increase in the discount rate used by the actuaries, which results in a decrease in the net present value of your share of the scheme liabilities.

findings.paper_title: The Audit Findings and SOA Report - 2024-25 (1)
findings.headline: Council's reserves projected to be exhausted by 2030/31 to cover identified revenue budget gap.
findings.detail: West Oxfordshire has identified a revenue budget gap in its Medium Term Financial Strategy. The council created a Budget Deficit Reserve and contributed £1.989m in 2024/25 specifically to fund this gap. The council acknowledges its reserves will only cover the deficit until 2030/31, after which point it faces acute financial stress.
findings.matters: A defined depletion date for reserves signals the end of the council's financial buffer and the timing of acute stress; 2030/31 gives a 5-6 year window before the council needs a structural solution to its revenue deficit.
findings.figures: £1.989m contributed to Budget Deficit Reserve in 2024/25; reserves depleted by 2030/31
findings.quote: with a level of reserves to fund budget deficits until they are potentially exhausted in 2030/31 as per the MTFS, updated in November 2025

findings.headline: Three prior-year audit recommendations on financial sustainability remain unresolved
findings.detail: The auditor has carried forward three recommendations from the predecessor auditor relating to (1) wider financial scenario planning in the MTFS, (2) focused development of planned savings and alternatives to reserves, and (3) adoption of a voluntary minimum threshold for unallocated general fund reserves. All three are marked ongoing/unresolved in the 2025 update.
findings.matters: Unresolved audit recommendations on the core drivers of financial sustainability (savings planning, scenario planning, reserve adequacy) suggest the council's response to known medium-term pressures may be insufficient. A lender needs assurance that the savings plan exists and is credible.
findings.figures: Three unresolved recommendations; no named savings figures or target provided in the report
findings.quote: We have three unresolved improvement recommendations, originally raised by the predecessor auditors

findings.headline: General Fund reserves will be drawn down to fund operations from 2026/27
findings.detail: The council expects to use its General Fund reserve to finance the cost of services from 2026/27 onwards due to the combination of the revenue stream losses and fair funding review impact. This is not sustainable medium-term and signals the council will be running down buffers.
findings.matters: Once reserves are consumed, a council cannot absorb shocks or fund necessary spending. A lender needs to know the trajectory of reserve depletion and when they are expected to run out.
findings.figures: General Fund will be used to finance services from 2026/27; the 2024/25 outturn shows contribution to reserves of £6,345k, suggesting reserves are still building, but MTFS assumes depletion begins in two years
findings.quote: It is therefore likely that the General Fund will be needed to finance the cost of services from 2026/27 to the foreseeable future

findings.headline: Fair Funding Review will significantly reduce business rates income from 2026/27
findings.detail: The government's fair funding review is expected to materially decrease the council's business rates income from 2026/27 onwards. This is a scheduled cut to a major revenue source with no named mitigation.
findings.matters: Business rates are a primary council revenue source; a known significant decrease from 2026/27 is a direct threat to financial sustainability unless met by identified savings or service reductions
findings.figures: Decrease from Fair Funding Review begins 2026/27
findings.quote: the outcome of the government's fair funding review will significantly decrease the Councils income from Business Rates from 2026/27

findings.headline: Three major revenue streams ending in 2025/26 with no replacement strategy named
findings.detail: The five-year MTFS assumes New Homes Bonus and Extended Producer Responsibility (Waste) payments both end in 2025/26. The council's budget has been relying on these; their loss creates a structural funding gap with no identified offset.
findings.matters: A lender is exposed if council operations depend on income sources that have a known expiry and no replacement savings plan. The auditor notes no significant weaknesses in financial sustainability, but this is an amber finding with unresolved recommendations on savings planning.
findings.figures: New Homes Bonus and Extended Producer Responsibility (Waste) payments end 2025/26
findings.quote: the five-year MTFS 2025/26 – 2029/30 which assumes that the new homes bonus and Extended Producer Responsibility (Waste) payments would end in 2025/26

findings.headline: Temporary emergency accommodation drove budget overspend despite treasury gains
findings.detail: The council's 2024/25 financial year was challenged by overspending on services, specifically temporary emergency accommodation. This was partly offset by treasury activities, resulting in a net contribution to reserves of £6,345k. However, the underlying service pressure is material.
findings.matters: Demand-driven overspends on homelessness services signal sustained cost pressure that treasury gains may not reliably cover; a lender needs to know if this is recurring or exceptional
findings.figures: £6,345k contribution to reserves (net after overspend); temporary accommodation was the named cost driver
findings.quote: The financial year had been challenging for the Council due to an overspend on services, arising from expenditure on temporary emergency accommodation, and worsened by the loss of the Housing Benefit Subsidy

news_drafts.headline: Pension contribution rate increasing from 17.6% to 20% from April 2026 following triennial revaluation, removing buffering secondary contributions
news_drafts.lead: This is a permanent, inflation-linked cost increase across the entire workforce with no offsetting reductions. The removal of secondary buffering exposes the council to future pension cost volatility.

news_drafts.headline: Temporary accommodation crisis: 73 households costing £924,000 per year in lost Housing Benefit subsidy, with £3m capital programme to solve it only 44% spent
news_drafts.lead: This is chronic revenue pressure that will persist until capital delivery completes (and even then, will only recover £361,000 of the £924,000 annual loss). The underspent capital programme shows housing acquisition targets are behind schedule, suggesting…

news_drafts.headline: Leisure contract income to drop by £1.39m annually from 2027/28 when the current contract ends, adding to the structural funding gap
news_drafts.lead: A £1.39m ongoing annual income loss from a service the council does not control (operated by a contractor) represents unrecoverable shrinkage in the revenue base and compounds the structural deficit.
